ideas.title: ChatGPT's CPM Collapse Is the Most Interesting Data Point in Advertising
ideas.trend: OpenAI launched a self-serve Ads Manager with CPC pricing this week after its initial $60 CPM fell to $25 in 10 weeks, targeting $2.5B in ad revenue for 2026.
ideas.consensus: OpenAI is diversifying revenue away from subscriptions and API by building a ChatGPT ad business, entering the same market as Google and Meta.
ideas.angle: The CPM collapse is not a failure signal — it is price discovery. The shift from CPM to CPC is the same format move Google made in 2000. The real structural question is whether conversational intent converts at a higher rate than search intent, which CPA tracking (live as of May 2026) will decide. If it does, the ceiling is above Google's $295B. If it does not, ChatGPT becomes the cheap CPC alternative.

content_pack.x_longform:
ChatGPT's ad pricing just told the market something Google spent 20 years learning: intent is worth what conversion data proves, and no platform has conversion data on day one.

In February, OpenAI launched ChatGPT advertising with a $60 CPM, a $200,000 minimum spend, and a first-wave roster that included Target, Ford, Expedia, and Adobe. Within ten weeks the CPM had fallen to $25. OpenAI scrapped the minimum entirely and shifted to cost-per-click pricing at $3 to $5.

That price move reflects the standard lifecycle of any new ad format. CPM is a brand awareness format. Advertisers pay it when they believe the attention is premium regardless of what the viewer does next. The collapse happened because no conversion data existed yet. Advertisers do not pay brand rates for performance-unknown inventory. They pay for clicks.

The shift to CPC is where this gets structurally interesting.

Google runs on CPC. Meta runs on CPC. In 2025 those two companies generated $295 billion and $196 billion in ad revenue respectively, almost entirely from performance-based CPC auctions. OpenAI moved onto the most validated ad pricing format in digital history.

The structural difference is intent.

Search intent is binary and late-funnel. "Best credit card for travel" is someone who has already decided to look. The word "best" is 20 seconds from a purchase decision. Google has documented those decision signals at scale across billions of daily searches for 25 years, which is why credit card companies pay $15 to $30 per search click.

Conversational intent is earlier, richer, and context-laden. "What credit card should I get for Tokyo in July, I already have an Amex, I want lounge access, and I am spending around $500 a year" tells ChatGPT the product category, the existing product in the wallet, the use case, the timing, and the price ceiling. Five decision variables in one message. A search box captures one.

Whether richer context converts at a higher rate is what CPA tracking will settle. OpenAI added CPA bidding in May alongside third-party measurement from Kargo, StackAdapt, Adobe, and Criteo. That is the infrastructure to close the conversion loop.

If ChatGPT clicks convert at twice the rate of search clicks, the CPC reprices upward from $3 to $15. If the conversion rate is lower, ChatGPT stays the cheap performance channel.

The scale projections: $2.5 billion target for 2026. One analyst projects $53 billion by 2029. OpenAI's stated ceiling is $100 billion by 2030. Google at $295 billion in 2025.

Getting from $2.5 billion to $100 billion in four years requires compounding at roughly 150% annually. Google took 25 years to reach $295 billion. The comparison looks unfavorable until you look at the funnel position.

If conversational intent sits above the search query in the decision funnel, ChatGPT captures the user before Google does. Earlier funnel position always has more leverage on the final decision.

If conversational intent replaces the search query entirely, ChatGPT is the search engine.

Google launched CPC pricing in 2000. The format that produced $295 billion in annual revenue was locked in during the first year. The next 25 years were compounding on top of a settled format.

OpenAI made its format shift in May. Ten weeks after launch.

Google sold the search window. OpenAI is selling the conversation before the search.

content_pack.substack_draft:
$60 CPM collapsed to $25 in ten weeks. That number is doing all the work in this story.

The conventional read is that ChatGPT's ad model stumbled. The reading that interests me more: it stumbled in exactly the way every new ad format stumbles before it becomes dominant. Google's AdWords launched in 2000 with CPM pricing. The shift to CPC came within the first year. The $295 billion in annual revenue arrived 25 years after that. The format shift was the hinge.

OpenAI made its own format shift in May, ten weeks in. CPC at $3 to $5, CPA bidding live, third-party measurement from Adobe and Criteo. The infrastructure to close the conversion loop is in place.

I am not yet sure whether conversational intent converts at a higher rate than search intent or a lower one. Nobody has the data yet. The CPA tracking that started this month is the beginning of that data. When conversion rates come in, the $25 CPM will either reprice toward $60 or settle as the permanent ceiling. That number, more than the revenue projections, is the one to watch.

ideas.title: NVIDIA Just Bought the Wire Factory
ideas.trend: NVIDIA announced up to $3.2B in Corning equity rights this week to expand optical fiber supply for AI data centers, sending Corning stock up 21% — its biggest gain since 2002.
ideas.consensus: NVIDIA is investing in US domestic manufacturing and AI infrastructure supply chains, diversifying beyond chip design.
ideas.angle: The GPU arms race has an underdiscussed constraint: moving data between chips. Copper wire maxes out at 2 meters; at 100,000-GPU data center scale the answer is co-packaged optics (fiber integrated into the GPU package). NVIDIA just locked up the optical fiber supply chain 18-24 months before every other hyperscaler hits the same bottleneck — the same pre-emption move TSMC made with wafer agreements before the 2021 chip shortage.

content_pack.x_longform:
NVIDIA just bought the wire factory.

Up to $3.2 billion in Corning equity rights and warrants. Three new manufacturing plants in North Carolina and Texas. Optical connectivity capacity expanded 10x. Fiber production up 50 percent. Corning gained 21 percent on the day, its biggest intraday move since 2002. NVIDIA gained 5 percent.

The real move is supply chain pre-emption, executed before the constraint becomes visible.

Data centers at the scale AI training requires hit a bottleneck that has nothing to do with the chip. Copper wire maxes out at roughly 2 meters. A modern GPU cluster at 100,000 units requires thousands of interconnects across distances copper cannot serve at the bandwidth AI workloads demand. The answer is co-packaged optics: optical fiber integrated directly into the GPU package. Corning makes the fiber. Scaling co-packaged optics across the next wave of hyperscaler data center builds requires 10x more optical connectivity supply than exists today.

NVIDIA locked up the supply chain 18 to 24 months before every other hyperscaler faces the same constraint.

The pattern is TSMC in 2019. TSMC locked in long-term wafer agreements before the 2021 chip shortage made the GPU queue visible to anyone outside a handful of supply chain analysts. Customers with wafer agreements kept building. Customers without paid 4x spot price or waited 18 months. TSMC signed because they priced the probability that the queue was coming.

NVIDIA knows the fiber queue is coming. GPU queue came first. Fiber queue is next.

Chips are the headline. Fiber is the constraint. The Corning warrants are NVIDIA's bet that the constraint is the business.

content_pack.substack_draft:
Most people are treating the NVIDIA-Corning deal as a manufacturing story. I think it is a supply chain pre-emption play, and the difference matters if you are trying to understand what actually determines who wins the AI infrastructure race long-term.

The pattern here is TSMC in 2019. TSMC began locking in long-term wafer agreements before the chip shortage was visible to anyone outside a handful of supply chain analysts. By 2021, when the GPU queue became a front-page story, customers with wafer agreements were building. Customers without them were waiting. TSMC had not predicted the shortage with certainty. They had priced the probability and signed accordingly.

NVIDIA just did the same thing with fiber. Co-packaged optics, optical fiber integrated at the chip package level, is the technical answer to the interconnect bottleneck that 100,000-GPU clusters create. Corning makes the fiber. NVIDIA secured up to $3.2 billion in rights to own part of the company that makes it.

I am not sure whether the fiber queue arrives on the same timeline as the GPU queue did. The technology adoption curve for co-packaged optics has more uncertainty in it than TSMC's wafer cycle did. But the shape of the move is identical, and the investors who understood TSMC's supply chain pre-emption in 2019 did not wait for certainty either.

ideas.title: David Autor Coined 'China Shock.' He Thinks the AI Parallel Is Wrong.
ideas.trend: Fortune and Bloomberg published competing economist analyses this week comparing AI job displacement to the China shock, with David Autor arguing the parallel fundamentally misreads the structure of AI disruption.
ideas.consensus: AI will displace workers the way China's manufacturing integration did — a broad macro shock that economists are now taking seriously after years of dismissal.
ideas.angle: The China shock had geography. Factory towns in Ohio had a zip code, and that zip code became a political fact. AI displaces cognitive functions across 50 states and 500 industries — no zip code, no concentrated political backlash. Nine million at-risk jobs dispersed everywhere is structurally different from one million factory jobs concentrated in 30 Midwestern counties. Dispersed damage is the optimist's case, not the pessimist's.

content_pack.x_longform:
David Autor coined the term "China shock." He thinks the AI parallel is wrong.

The China shock had geography. Factory towns in Ohio and Michigan were on a map, and political backlash followed the map. AI displaces cognitive functions, not zip codes. Per the American AI Jobs Risk Index, nine million US jobs are at risk, spread across 50 states and 500 industries.

Apollo's Torsten Slok argues dispersed disruption makes AI more similar to the China shock, not less. Both lower costs, raise productivity, and displace workers who cannot retrain fast enough. Fortune published the analysis this week.

Dispersed damage across 500 industries is easier to absorb than concentrated damage across 30 counties. That is also, quietly, the optimist's case.

content_pack.substack_draft:
Most people I talk to about AI job displacement treat the China shock as the natural reference point. The more I read about it, the more the comparison feels like it gets one critical thing wrong.

The China shock had geography. Deindustrialization hollowed out factory towns in specific counties. David Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon Hanson mapped the casualties to specific congressional districts and showed that trade exposure correlated with political radicalization over a decade. The damage had a zip code. That zip code became a political fact.

AI displaces cognitive functions. A paralegal in New York, an accountant in Omaha, a customer service rep in Phoenix. The American AI Jobs Risk Index puts nine million US jobs at risk, distributed across 50 states. The damage has no single zip code. No single congressional district absorbs enough of it to become a political organizing point in the same way.

I am genuinely uncertain whether that diffusion makes the AI shock more or less dangerous than the China shock. Dispersed harm is harder to organize around politically, which might mean less backlash and faster adaptation. Or it might mean the same scale of harm in a form that is harder to name and therefore harder to address.
